name: spim
why: A MIPS32 simulator that lets you watch assembly execute step by step, a classic door into how processors run code.

brief.what_it_is: SPIM is a self-contained simulator that reads and executes MIPS32 assembly language programs. It provides a simple debugger and a minimal set of operating system services. It does not execute binary (compiled) programs, so the input is assembly source and the output is the program's behavior in the simulator. It has a terminal interface (the spim program) and windowed interfaces (QtSpim, plus the older xspim and PCSpim). It implements almost the entire MIPS32 assembler-extended instruction set, but omits most floating point comparisons, rounding modes, and the memory system page tables.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no explicit motivation beyond describing the tool as a simulator for MIPS32 programs. Its author is James Larus, who writes that SPIM is no longer supported and that the code has been stable for many years.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internals. It says Spim reads and executes assembly language programs for the MIPS32 processor, provides a simple debugger, and supplies a minimal set of operating system services. Spim ships with complete source code and documentation.
brief.install_notes: The homepage does not mention Homebrew. Prebuilt, immediately installable QtSpim packages for Microsoft Windows, Mac OS X, and Linux are downloaded from https://sourceforge.net/projects/spimsimulator/files/. Building QtSpim from source requires the Qt framework, available from http://qt-project.org/downloads. The page does not describe first-run steps or configuration.
brief.standout: The same QtSpim source and user interface run on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and the project is self-contained with complete source and documentation. Its scope is deliberately narrow: it runs assembly source for MIPS32 and does not attempt full MIPS64 or other processor variants.
brief.status: quiet. The README says "Spim is no longer supported" and that the author is retiring, inviting people to fork it. It also says QtSpim is "currently being maintained," which conflicts with the retirement note, and the page shows no release date or commit history. The copyright line reads 1990-2023, which is the most recent dated evidence on the page.
brief.caveats: The author states the project is no longer supported, and the older versions (xspim, PCSpim) are no longer maintained. It runs only assembly source and cannot run compiled binaries. It is not a full MIPS64 simulator. It omits most floating point comparisons and rounding modes and the memory system page tables. The license is BSD. Building QtSpim from source needs the Qt framework. The homepage was reachable and read in full; no other links were followed.
quotes: Spim is a self-contained simulator that runs MIPS32 programs.
Spim does not execute binary (compiled) programs.

Spim is no longer supported. The code has been stable for many years, with a few occasional bugs. But, as I reach retirement, it is clear to me that Spim should retire as well. Feel free to fork a copy and fix the bugs yourself!
